newsitem.title: USA: Smithfield Foods profits up, Hormel net unchanged.
newsitem.headline: Smithfield Foods profits up, Hormel net unchanged.

text.p: Smithfield Foods Inc. Thursday reported a sharp rise in quarterly earnings, boosted by high pork prices, but Hormel Foods Corp., maker of Spam processed meat, said the high pork prices stifled any growth in profits.

Smithfield, based in Norfolk, Va., said its net income jumped to $15.7 million, or 82 cents per share, for the third quarter ended Jan. 26, from $8.7 million, or 46 cents per share, in the year-ago period.
The hog producer, pork processor and pork and processed meats marketer said sales rose to $1.08 billion from $687.0 million.
The latest results include income from continuing operations of $10.8 million, and a loss from discontinued operations of $2.1 million.
Smithfield attributed its gains mainly to the inclusion of John Morrell & Co.'s results for the third full quarter and a surge in profits at the company's hog production group.
Smithfield acquired John Morrell in December 1995.

Somewhat offsetting these factors were sharply lower fresh pork profits, a loss at Lykes Meat Group which was acquired in November 1996, and weather-related plant shutdowns and inefficiencies at John Morrell in January.
"We have sharply reduced operating costs at Lykes and have been able to increase both its domestic and international business," said Joseph Luter, chairman of Smithfield.
"As a result, we expect that Lykes will be operating profitably by the end of the current fiscal year."
Smithfield's brands include Smithfield Premium, John Morrell, Lykes, Jamestown, Kretschmar, Dinner Bell, Realean, Patrick's Pride, Tobin's First Prize, Valleydale and Sunnyland.
Hormel reported earnings of $20.98 million, or 27 cents a share, in the first quarter, barely changed from $20.67, or 27 cents a share, in the year-ago period.
Sales rose to $810.3 million from $724.4 million, due in part to higher selling prices for the company's products.
Hormel, based in Austin, Minn., said higher than normal pork raw material costs will continue to be a challenge, even though a gradual increase in pork supplies is expected.
Joel Johnson, chairman, said grain costs, mainly corn, have eased considerably, reducing costs in the future for Hormel's Jennie-O Foods Inc. subsidiary.
"However, prices for pork, the company's primary raw material, remain high due to reduced hog numbers and significant increases in industry-wide slaughter capacity," he said.
Smithfield's stock rose $1.50 to $36.125 on Nasdaq in afternoon trading. Hormel edged up 62.5 cents to $25 on the New York Stock Exchange.
